question.title: Worktree Isolation for Parallel Tasks
question.scenario: A senior engineer uses Claude Code to work on three features simultaneously in a large monorepo. They find that switching branches between tasks causes Claude to lose context and mix up changes from different features. They want each task to have its own isolated file state while sharing the same Git history. The engineer is evaluating worktree-based isolation versus other approaches.
question.question-text: Why is git worktree-based isolation the preferred approach for running parallel Claude Code tasks on the same repository?

choices.choice: Worktrees are faster than cloning because they copy only the files Claude has modified
Worktrees allow Claude Code to merge changes from multiple features automatically without conflicts
Worktrees enable Claude Code to run in a different programming language context per task

Worktrees provide separate working directories with independent file state and branch checkouts while sharing the same .git object store, preventing cross-task file contamination without duplicating repository data

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about what Git feature lets multiple branches be checked out simultaneously in separate directories, sharing one underlying repo.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Git worktrees create separate working directory checkouts that share the same underlying .git object store. Each worktree can be on a different branch with its own file state, so changes in one task don't affect another. This is ideal for parallel Claude Code sessions because each session operates in its own directory with no risk of cross-contamination. Unlike full clones, worktrees don't duplicate the object store, saving disk space and setup time. They don't automatically merge changes or change language contexts — those are unrelated capabilities. The key benefit is isolation without duplication.

ul.li: Each Claude Code session launched in a worktree directory gets its own CLAUDE.md context (if the worktree contains one), enabling task-specific instructions for each parallel feature.

Worktree isolation is particularly valuable in CI/CD scenarios where multiple Claude Code agents process different tasks concurrently — each agent gets a clean filesystem view without race conditions on file modifications.
When combining worktrees with Claude Code's /compact or conversation management, each worktree session maintains its own conversation history, preventing context bleed between unrelated features.

question.title: Handling Partial and Malformed Output
question.scenario: A real-time data extraction pipeline uses Claude to process streaming news articles and extract structured event records. The pipeline uses streaming API responses so it can begin processing before Claude finishes generating. Occasionally, network interruptions or max_tokens limits cause truncated responses. The team needs a resilient parsing strategy that handles partial output gracefully.
question.question-text: What is the best strategy for handling truncated or partial structured output from Claude's streaming API in a production pipeline?

choices.choice: Use a streaming JSON parser that processes tokens incrementally, detect truncation via the stop_reason field (checking for "end_turn" vs "max_tokens"), and for truncated responses either salvage complete records from the partial output or trigger a continuation request
Set max_tokens to a very large value so truncation never happens
Buffer the entire streamed response before parsing so truncation is never an issue
Switch from JSON to CSV output since CSV rows are independently parseable even if the stream is cut off

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider how the pipeline can detect whether the model finished normally or was cut off, and how to extract value from incomplete output.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A resilient streaming pipeline should: (1) use an incremental JSON parser that can extract complete objects from a partial stream, (2) check the stop_reason field to distinguish between natural completion ("end_turn") and truncation ("max_tokens"), and (3) for truncated responses, either salvage fully-formed records from the partial output or send a continuation request asking Claude to resume from where it was cut off. Buffering the entire response defeats the purpose of streaming. Setting very large max_tokens doesn't prevent network interruptions and wastes token budget. CSV seems simpler but loses the hierarchical structure that JSON provides and introduces its own escaping and quoting complexities.

ul.li: When designing for continuation, include the partial output in the next request's assistant prefill so Claude can seamlessly continue the JSON structure from the exact point of truncation — this avoids duplicate records or structural breaks.

A streaming JSON parser like jsonstream or ijson can emit complete objects as they are parsed from the stream, allowing the pipeline to process finished records (e.g., the first 8 of 10 events) even if the final records are truncated.

For critical pipelines, implement a "completeness check" that verifies the expected number of records against a count field emitted early in the output (e.g., "total_events": 10 as the first field), so the system knows when truncation caused data loss versus when all records were delivered.

question.title: XML vs JSON Output Pattern Selection
question.scenario: A content management team uses Claude for two distinct tasks: (1) extracting metadata fields (title, author, date, tags) from blog posts into a database, and (2) generating editorial markup where sections of text need annotations like "needs citation," "tone too informal," or "factual claim — verify." The team is debating whether to standardize on JSON for both tasks or use different output formats.
question.question-text: Which output format strategy best fits the two distinct use cases described?

choices.choice: Use YAML for both tasks since it's the most human-readable structured format
Use XML for both tasks since it supports both structured data and inline annotations

Use JSON (via tool-use) for the metadata extraction task where you need typed fields conforming to a database schema, and use XML for the editorial markup task where annotations need to be interleaved within the source text
Use JSON for both tasks since it's the universal data interchange format

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about whether these two tasks have the same structural needs — does one require wrapping annotations around flowing text?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The two tasks have fundamentally different output structure needs. Metadata extraction produces flat or nested key-value data that maps perfectly to JSON, and using tool-use provides schema enforcement for the database. Editorial markup, however, requires annotations to be embedded within flowing text — wrapping phrases with tags like <annotation type="needs-citation">some claim</annotation> — which is XML's native strength. JSON is awkward for inline text annotation because you'd need to split text into fragments and wrap each in objects. Standardizing on one format forces an unnatural fit for one of the two tasks. YAML adds parsing complexity without meaningful benefits over JSON for these use cases.

ul.li: Claude is naturally skilled at producing XML-style inline annotations because its training data includes extensive HTML and XML markup, making it reliable at opening and closing tags around relevant text spans.
For the JSON metadata task, tool-use schemas can enforce enum constraints (e.g., tags must come from an allowed list) and required fields, providing validation that prompt-based XML cannot match.

A practical pattern for the annotation task is to ask Claude to return the original text with XML annotation tags inserted, then use an XML parser to extract both the annotations and their positions — this preserves the original text while adding a structured annotation layer.

question.title: Escalation to Human Reviewers
question.scenario: A large e-commerce company has deployed a Claude-powered agent that handles refund requests. The agent can autonomously approve refunds up to $50 and generate templated responses. For requests over $50 or those involving suspected fraud, the agent should escalate to a human reviewer. The team notices that the agent sometimes approves borderline cases autonomously when the user is persistent, and other times escalates trivially simple low-value requests unnecessarily.
question.question-text: Which design change would MOST effectively improve the escalation accuracy of this refund agent?

choices.choice: Add more emphatic language to the system prompt telling Claude to "strictly follow the $50 rule no matter what"
Remove the agent's ability to approve any refunds and route all requests to human reviewers

Implement the escalation decision as a programmatic rule in the orchestration layer based on structured data extracted by Claude, rather than letting Claude make the escalation decision in natural language
Train the agent with examples of persistent users so it learns to resist social pressure

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which part of the decision — understanding the request versus enforcing the business rule — is best handled by the model versus by code.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Moving the escalation decision into deterministic code in the orchestration layer ensures that policy rules (refund amount thresholds, fraud signals) are enforced consistently regardless of conversational pressure. Claude's role becomes extracting structured data (refund amount, reason, fraud indicators) which the orchestrator then evaluates against hard-coded rules. Emphatic prompting (A) is unreliable against persistent or cleverly phrased requests. Removing all autonomy (B) eliminates the agent's value proposition. Training with examples (D) may help but cannot guarantee deterministic policy compliance. The key insight is that business rules should live in code, not in prompts.

ul.li: The "extract then decide" pattern is a foundational principle in production agent design: use the LLM for understanding and extraction, use deterministic code for policy enforcement and routing.
This architecture is also more auditable -- you can log both the extracted data and the rule evaluation separately, making it easy to diagnose why any particular case was escalated or approved.
Anthropic recommends using tool-use responses with defined schemas to enforce structured extraction, which naturally separates the extraction step from the decision step.

question.title: Idempotent Tool Calls in Multi-Step Agents
question.scenario: A multi-agent research system uses Claude to gather data from external APIs, synthesize findings, and write reports. The agent executes tool calls to query databases and POST results to a reporting service. During a network interruption, the orchestrator loses connection mid-workflow and must resume. Some tool calls may have already executed successfully but the orchestrator did not receive confirmation. The architect must ensure resumption does not cause duplicate side effects.
question.question-text: Which design pattern BEST ensures safe resumption of this multi-step workflow without duplicate side effects?

choices.choice: Assign a unique idempotency key to each tool call, persist the key and result before execution, and on resume check whether each tool call has already completed before executing it
Set the Claude API temperature to 0 to guarantee identical outputs on replay, then re-run from the start
Re-run the entire workflow from the beginning, since Claude will generate the same tool calls deterministically
Skip all tool calls that might have executed and only run the remaining steps, accepting possible gaps in data

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about how the orchestrator can tell whether a tool call already executed successfully before the crash, even if it never received the confirmation.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Assigning unique idempotency keys to each tool call and persisting their execution state creates a checkpoint system that allows safe resumption. On recovery, the orchestrator checks each tool call's key: if already executed, it reuses the stored result; if not, it executes normally. Re-running from scratch (A) is unsafe because Claude is not deterministic (even at temperature 0, outputs are not guaranteed identical) and because external APIs may create duplicates. Temperature 0 (B) does not guarantee determinism due to batching and floating-point differences, and even if it did, the external API calls would still duplicate. Skipping potentially-executed calls (C) loses data integrity.

ul.li: The idempotency pattern for agent tool calls follows the same principle as payment processing: write-ahead logging of intent, execution, and confirmation creates a recoverable state machine.
For read-only tool calls (database queries), idempotency is naturally safe -- the key concern is write operations (POSTs, updates, deletes) where duplication causes real harm.

Production agent frameworks often implement a "tool execution ledger" that records: tool name, parameters hash, idempotency key, execution status, and result -- enabling both safe retry and full audit trails.

question.title: Partial Failure in Multi-Step Extraction
question.scenario: A structured data extraction pipeline processes incoming contracts by sending each contract to Claude in three sequential steps: (1) extract party names and dates, (2) extract financial terms, (3) extract obligations and deadlines. Step 1 and Step 2 succeed, but Step 3 fails with a 500 Internal Server Error after two retries. The pipeline processes hundreds of contracts per day and must maintain high throughput.
question.question-text: How should the pipeline handle this partial failure scenario?

choices.choice: Save the successful results from Steps 1 and 2 with a status marker indicating Step 3 is incomplete, place the contract in a retry queue for Step 3 only, and proceed to the next contract
Halt the entire pipeline until the 500 error is resolved to prevent any incomplete data from being stored
Discard all results from Steps 1 and 2 and re-queue the entire contract for reprocessing from scratch
Return the partial results from Steps 1 and 2 as the final output and mark the contract as complete

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the cost of re-doing successful work versus the risk of storing incomplete data — how would you balance both concerns?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Saving partial results with a clear status marker and retrying only the failed step is the optimal approach. It preserves the work already done (avoiding redundant API calls and costs), maintains data integrity through explicit status tracking, and keeps the pipeline moving for other contracts. Discarding all results (A) wastes successful work and increases API costs. Marking incomplete data as complete (C) silently loses information and violates data integrity. Halting the entire pipeline (D) lets one failure block all other processing, which is unacceptable at high throughput. The checkpoint pattern enables both efficiency and correctness.

ul.li: Production extraction pipelines should model each document as a state machine with explicit states: queued, step-1-complete, step-2-complete, complete, and failed-at-step-N -- enabling targeted retries and progress monitoring.
A dead-letter queue should capture contracts that fail repeatedly (after max retries), routing them to human review rather than retrying indefinitely.
500 errors from the Claude API indicate a server-side issue and are transient -- they are safe to retry, unlike 400-level errors which typically indicate a problem with the request itself.

question.title: Confidence Thresholds for Escalation
question.scenario: A legal technology company has built a Claude-based contract review agent that identifies risky clauses and classifies them by severity (low, medium, high). The agent processes thousands of contracts per week. The legal team wants to review only the contracts that truly need human attention, but they cannot afford to miss genuinely high-risk clauses. The team is debating how to set the confidence threshold for escalation to human review.
question.question-text: Which threshold strategy BEST balances thoroughness with reviewer efficiency for this contract review system?

choices.choice: Escalate everything classified as medium or high risk regardless of confidence, ensuring humans see all potentially risky clauses

Use asymmetric thresholds: escalate high-risk classifications at a low confidence bar (e.g., 60%) to avoid missing dangers, but require high confidence (e.g., 90%) before autonomously marking a contract as low-risk and skipping human review
Set a single high confidence threshold (e.g., 95%) -- only escalate when the agent is very confident a clause is high-risk, minimizing the volume of human reviews
Let the legal team manually set thresholds per contract type without providing a default, since risk tolerance varies

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider whether the consequences of missing a real risk and the consequences of an unnecessary review are equally severe for this use case.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Asymmetric thresholds correctly reflect the asymmetric costs in legal review. Missing a genuinely high-risk clause (false negative) could expose the company to significant legal liability, so the bar for escalation should be low -- even moderate suspicion warrants human eyes. Conversely, the bar for autonomously clearing a contract should be high, because incorrectly skipping review is the dangerous failure mode. A single high threshold (A) optimizes for reviewer efficiency at the cost of safety. Escalating everything medium+ (B) overwhelms reviewers and defeats the purpose of automation. Deferring entirely to per-type manual configuration (D) provides no safe default and risks misconfiguration.

ul.li: Asymmetric thresholds mirror the concept of "sensitivity vs. specificity" in medical testing -- for high-consequence domains, you optimize for sensitivity (catching all true positives) even at the cost of more false positives.

The confidence scores from Claude can be obtained by asking the model to rate its confidence explicitly in a structured response, or by analyzing logprobs where available -- but these should be calibrated against ground truth before relying on specific numeric thresholds.

Over time, the thresholds can be tuned using feedback data: track which escalated contracts actually required human intervention and which were false alarms, then adjust thresholds to optimize the precision-recall tradeoff for the specific domain.
